segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: i want to take you to a roadside diner. bottomless coffee, plastic seats. three guys who are sick of their day jobs, one of them's called jensen, and they've convinced themselves that the sort of graphics a film studio pays a fortune for could live in your kid's bedroom computer. who'd pay. people playing games. everyone told them that was a ridiculous reason to start a business.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: six years later they've got a hit and they coin a term for it that we all still use, the g p u, the first one ever sold. it's so good that bill gates's lot come calling, they need something to power this console they're building, and they wire over two hundred million in advance. magazines are naming them business of the year. that could have been the whole story.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: instead they had this weird side project. a phd from stanford, ian, had figured out you could trick a graphics card into doing ordinary maths. and the trick is useful because inside there aren't a few clever brains, there's thousands of simple ones going off together, like the ones flashing on the wall behind me. so they packaged it up, named it cuda, charged nobody a penny and shipped it in everything.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: you can guess how shareholders took that. gamers weren't asking for it, it made the product dearer to make, and it swallowed hundreds of millions each year with zero to show. two thousand and eight, the share price falls off a cliff. five years after that there's an agitator buying in and asking why are we still paying for this. meanwhile the top line barely moves.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: what changed everything was a contest. you show a computer a photo and it has to say what's in it, a cat, a lorry, whatever. the best software on earth was getting about a quarter of them wrong. in twenty twelve a toronto student turns up with two cards you'd buy for playing call of duty and knocks that down to fifteen percent. overnight, everybody doing ai had to switch over.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: right, so why does everyone still end up buying from them, and i'd say there's four reasons stacked on top of each other and a rival has got to crack the lot in one go. the first is the hardware itself, and here's the funny thing, theirs isn't even the best on paper. amd's newest has half as much memory again and undercuts them, and still sells about one twelfth as much into server farms.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: because what people are really buying is what sits on top. you know how if you've got an iphone everything just talks to everything else. it's that. millions of developers grew up on it, there's a ready made library for anything you can think of, and it's all free. the competition's equivalent came along nearly a decade late. so when somebody in a lab has a eureka moment, guess which one they've coded it for.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: then there's the wiring in between. the models have got so big that no single processor can hold them, so it's all about how fast they can talk to each other. nvidia puts seventy two in a cupboard and makes them behave like one. and they were smart enough to snap up mellanox before anyone cared about networking, and that purchase pays for itself several times over every single year now.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: and finally, good luck getting anything made. the top end of the chip world runs through one manufacturer on one island off the coast of china. and it's not even the chip that's the hold up, it's gluing the pieces together at the end. somewhere around six in every ten slots for that are already spoken for, by these guys. you could have a better design and nowhere to build it.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: so who's had a proper go. the closest is google, who've thrown over ten years and an eye watering amount of money at it. the other cloud giants have all got something in the works. and here's my favourite part, every single one of them still places orders with nvidia. around eighty cents of each dollar anyone spends on ai processors ends up in the same place.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: some of you lived through the late nineties and i can see the look on your faces. so compare it with the other great building sprees in the states, as a slice of the whole economy. the highway system, one point one. cabling up the internet, one point four. the railroad barons, two point two. and what's being planned for ai between now and twenty thirty two is bigger than any of them, over three and a half.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: does it actually do anything, though, beyond writing your emails. well, stockholm gave it a nobel two years ago, for cracking protein structures and inventing ones that never existed. it took a new lung medicine from a blank page to patients in roughly half the usual time. and if you're a woman getting screened in sweden there's a better chance they'll spot the cancer, with the reading load on the doctors cut nearly in half.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: and once it can pick a lock by itself, which google says it now can, with no person involved at any point, it stops being a tech story and turns into a defence one. that's how the two big capitals see it. china has set itself a deadline of twenty thirty to be top dog. america won't let its best processors be shipped over there. neither of them is going to ease off.

segments.speaker: Rob
segments.say: so that's my case. best silicon, best code, best plumbing, first in the queue at the factory. everyone with money and everyone with an army is building on it, and unless human beings give up on progress i can't see what stops it. that's the story. the question for you is whether the books agree with the story, and for that, here's panshul.
